text:
In this module, you've explored how to build evaluators
and test whether you can trust their judgments.

You started with code evaluators for requirements that can
be checked directly.

Then you looked at LLM judges for requirements that
need interpretation.
You also wrote a rubric for an application-specific requirement,

and you measured whether the judge's labels agreed with reviewed
labels before relying on them.

Now, let's bring those ideas together with the Northwind agent.
In this module's lab, you'll use three evaluators.

One checks whether the products mentioned in a
response actually exist.

The second one checks whether the response correctly answers the
customer's question,

and the third one checks whether the response stays within
Northwind's capabilities.

Each evaluator answers a different question,
so you'll keep their results separate.

That way, when a response fails, you can see which
requirement it failed.
Take a look at the reviewed cases from the Northwind benchmark.

Each case keeps together the customer's question, the agent's
response, and the label a reviewer assigned to that response.

That label matters because it applies to the specific
response that was reviewed.

Before you build the evaluators, set aside some of those reviewed
cases as a held-out validation set.

Use the remaining development cases to build
and refine the evaluators.

Save the held-out set for later, when you want to test whether the
evaluators work on examples that did not shape how they were built.
When you choose the held-out validation cases, think about coverage.

Suppose responses that go beyond Northwind's capabilities are
rare in the benchmark.

If you split the data randomly, your validation set may contain only
one or two of those cases.
Then missing one policy violation would change recall a lot,

and you still would not have much evidence about whether the judge
catches that failure reliably.

So include enough reviewed examples of the important failure
types you want to test.
That doesn't mean those failures are equally common in production.

It means your validation set is designed to test whether the
evaluator can catch them.
Now, choose evaluators for the three Northwind requirements.

First, every product mentioned in an agent response should exist in
the catalog. is your source of truth, so this is a code evaluator.

If the customer asks for a jacket and the agent recommends a product
that is not in the catalog, the answer may sound reasonable,
but the product does not exist.

The evaluator can compare the product names or IDs in the response
with the catalog. The check passes if every mentioned product exists.

If the response mentions a product that is not in the catalog,
it fails. You don't need an LLM to decide that.
The catalog comparison determines the result.

But a response can mention only real products and still fail to answer
the customer's question.

For example, the customer might ask which shoes are
best for rainy weather,

and the agent might list real products without explaining
which ones are waterproof or appropriate for rain.

The products exist, but the response may not answer
the actual question.

To evaluate that, you need to interpret the customer's question
and the agent's response together.
This is a good place to use a built-in correctness evaluator.

Phoenix provides a CorrectnessEvaluator for common response quality
judgments like accuracy, completeness, and logical consistency.

You provide the customer question and the agent response, and the
judge decides whether the response correctly answers the question.

So now you have two checks: one code evaluator that asks,
"Are the products real?"

and one correctness judge that asks, "Did the response answer the
customer's question?"

But the Northwind agent has another requirement that general
correctness does not fully capture, which has to do with scope.

It can answer product and catalog questions, but it should not look up
orders, process returns, issue refunds, check shipping status,
or access other support systems.

If a customer asks, "Can I return this after 60 days?" the agent
should not invent a return window or ask for an order number.

It should simply explain that it cannot help with returns.
A general correctness evaluator may not know that boundary.

It might see a fluent, helpful-sounding return answer
and treat it as acceptable.

But for Northwind, that response is outside the agent's capabilities.
That means this requirement needs a custom LLM judge.

You'll build that judge using the rubric structure from
earlier in the module.

Start with the role: the judge is evaluating whether a Northwind
customer-support response stays within the agent's capabilities.

Then, define the criteria: a compliant response stays within product
and catalog support.

If the customer asks for something outside those capabilities, a
compliant response says that Northwind cannot help with that request.

A non-compliant response invents a process or capability
that the agent was never given.

That could be a return policy, a refund process, a shipping lookup,
or a support channel that does not exist in the provided information.

Next, provide the inputs. For this evaluator,
the judge needs the customer's question and the agent's response.

Put them in a clearly labeled data block so the judge knows exactly
what it is evaluating. Then add reviewed development examples.

Choose examples that clarify the boundary between compliant
and non-compliant responses.

For example, one compliant response might say, "I can help with
product and catalog questions, but I can't process returns."

A non-compliant response might say, "You have 90 days to return the
item," even though Northwind never provided that policy.

Finally, constrain the output. Ask for one label:
COMPLIANT or NON_COMPLIANT.

Fixed labels make the results easier to compare with reviewed labels,
and easier to filter in Phoenix.

Once you have the three evaluators, run them on the development cases
and save each result as a separate annotation.

That part is important because a response can pass one requirement
and fail another. Suppose a customer asks about returning an item.

The agent mentions only real Northwind products,
It gives a response that sounds complete and helpful,
but it also invents a return process that Northwind does not support.

The product_exists evaluator may pass, as well as the correctness
evaluator, but the policy_compliance judge should fail.

If you collapse those results into one overall score,
that policy failure can disappear.

Separate annotations let you see which requirement failed and
which responses need inspection.

Before relying on the policy compliance labels,
validate the custom judge.
Run it on the held-out set,

and compare its COMPLIANT and NON_COMPLIANT predictions with the
reviewed labels for those same responses.
Use recall to see how many actual policy violations the judge caught.

Check precision to measure how often its policy
violation flags were correct,

and use Cohen's kappa to check how much the judge agrees with the
reviewed labels beyond what you would expect by chance.

But don't stop at the metrics. When the judge and reviewer disagree,
open the case and inspect it.

Read the customer question, the agent response,
and the judge's explanation. Then apply the rubric yourself.

What if the judge missed that the response invented a refund process,
or the reviewed label was wrong,
or maybe the rubric did not make the capability boundary clear enough?

A disagreement does not automatically tell you which side is right,
it tells you where to look.

If you revise the rubric based on those disagreements,
change one thing at a time,
then test the revised version on fresh reviewed cases when you can.

Once a case has influenced the rubric, it is no longer a clean
validation case for that revised evaluator.
Keep the same discipline you used earlier in the module.

Build on development cases, validate on held-out cases,
inspect disagreements, revise carefully, then test again.
That is the process you'll use in the upcoming lab.

Define the requirement, identify the evidence that can answer it,
choose the simplest evaluator that can apply the requirement reliably.

Use code when the answer can be checked directly. Use a built-in LLM
judge when the requirement is interpretive, but general.

Use a custom rubric when the requirement depends on
application-specific rules.

And with that, you're nearing the end of Module 3,
where you've focused mostly on evaluating individual responses.
In the next module, you'll widen the view.

You'll evaluate what happens along the way, the actions an agent
chooses, the tools it calls, the sequence it follows,
and the state it changes outside the conversation.
Good luck with the lab, and see you in Module 4.
